acts.title: The Wax Account — Scribe's Port
acts.desc: The scribe's port after the narration at Alcinous's court. The scribe who took dictation holds a chest: the wax tablets of Odysseus's account of the Sirens — including the passages where Odysseus said he could not continue in the usual form, and the scribe recorded those interruptions too. The account is already incomplete; the gaps are part of it. Insight DC 12.
acts.passText: The Fighter takes the tablets with both hands. The scribe exhales.
acts.failText: The Fighter asks about the content. The scribe is not going to discuss the content. After a silence he pushes the tablets forward again. TOKEN granted — but the scribe doesn't exhale; he just stops being in the room as quickly as possible.

acts.title: The Wax Account — Port Road
acts.desc: A traveling sophist on the port road has heard the tablets exist. He wants to copy them for his school — he calls them 'the most significant piece of experiential philosophy since Tiresias.' The tablets are not the Sirens' song; they are Odysseus's account of what a bound man could receive of it. Copying them without this context would produce exactly the wrong effect. Persuasion DC 13.
acts.passText: The scholar notes the argument and lets the Fighter pass, though he is clearly planning to visit the archive.
acts.failText: He follows, arguing. A delay of half a day before he finally accepts the argument in its reframed form. The tablets are not touched.

acts.title: The Wax Account — PRT Approach
acts.desc: A thick, weathered sailor waits at the dock's entrance — he served at the oars the day they passed the Sirens, ears stopped with wax. He has been waiting three days. The tablets are not what the Sirens sang; they are what Odysseus understood while bound, filtered through memory and a scribe's hand. The sailor is asking for something the tablets cannot give him. Persuasion DC 14; combat 2× AC 13 HP 16 if failed.
acts.passText: The tablets arrive intact.
acts.failText: One corner tablet takes a glancing blow; the corner wax is chipped; the text in that corner is partially illegible. At the archive, the Archivus notes: the damaged corner is one of the scribe's interpolated passages, not Odysseus's dictation. The gap made by the corner-chip is another place where the account stops.

acts.title: The Wax Account — Harbor Loading Dock
acts.desc: Harbor loading dock. The tablets must be loaded onto the ship for the northern crossing. A rough crossing is expected; wax softens with heat and impact. Athletics DC 13 to secure the chest without damage.
acts.passText: The chest is secured and the tablets arrive at Weimar intact.
acts.failText: The crossing is rougher than expected. One tablet face softens slightly at a corner. The text is readable. Sweelinck notes it as a boundary condition.

acts.title: The Wax Account — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive intake. File the Wax Account — Odysseus's partial account of the Sirens' song, including the passages where the account fails. The gaps are not defects but boundary conditions: the bound man's record of survivable knowledge. Insight DC 12.
acts.passText: Sweelinck reads the gaps as carefully as the text. 'The places where he said he could not continue,' he says. 'Those are the record.' He files it under Limits of Transmission — First Entry.
acts.failText: Filed under Odyssean Narration, Alcinous Court. The tablets are in the archive.

acts.title: Iphitus's Provenance — Dexithea's Decision
acts.desc: Notary Konon's house in Messenia. Dexithea, Iphitus's granddaughter, has the attestation in front of her — the document that confirms Iphitus gave the bow to Odysseus as a guest-gift, which would classify it as xenia property and remove it from the suitors' contest. She is asking whether the filing changes what the friendship was. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: You tell her the document preserves the fact that Iphitus gave the bow to a friend. It does not change what that was. She signs. She says: 'My grandfather told me they never got to share a table.' She folds her hands.
acts.failText: She signs without getting the answer she needed. The attestation is complete. But she does not look at the Fighter again.

acts.title: Iphitus's Provenance — Inspection Writ
acts.desc: The Messenian road. A Lacedaemonian official with a writ covering documents relating to the Ithaca dispute reads the carrier as an agent of the interested party. The distinction between neutral carrier and agent is the argument. INT DC 12.
acts.passText: You name the distinction. He accepts it. He notes 'neutral carrier, uncontested transit' and waves you through.
acts.failText: He notes the document in his log and releases it — the carrier's status is disputed but the document itself is authorized for transit. The notation may require explanation at the registry.

acts.title: Iphitus's Provenance — Delay Offer
acts.desc: The harbor tavern. A representative of three suitors' families offers significant coin for a two-day delay. He is not explaining the legal consequence: a two-day delay lets the suitors' preliminary filing close first, making the attestation a minority view. Persuasion DC 13.
acts.passText: You say: if the suitors' preliminary filing closes first, the attestation becomes a minority view. You can see he knows you understand this. He pays for your drink and leaves.
acts.failText: You decline without fully naming what he offered. He nods, finishes his cup, and leaves. He will try a different approach.

acts.title: Iphitus's Provenance — Dock Ambush
acts.desc: Two hired men at the Ithaca harbor. They want the document, not its destruction — but the seal must remain intact. Combat 2× AC 13 HP 22.
acts.passText: Both men are down. The seal is unbroken.
acts.failText: They take the document and hold it in a warehouse. You find it three hours later. The seal is intact. They didn't open it — they only needed the delay.

acts.title: Iphitus's Provenance — Ithaca Registry
acts.desc: Polyphron at the Ithaca estate registry desk. The suitors' preliminary filing is in the pending column. He asks about the custody chain. WIS DC 11: reconstruct the chain from Dexithea's stylus to this desk in the precise form the prior-category rule requires.
acts.passText: Polyphron writes 'prior category established: guest-friendship property, xenia obligations attached.' He stamps it with the date and time. The suitors' preliminary filing moves to the secondary column. 'The bow,' he says, 'was never their property to contest with.'
acts.failText: Polyphron flags the carrier-writ notation from Act II and files both documents as co-equal, pending adjudicator review. The attestation is in the record. The prior-category ruling will require a separate proceeding.

acts.title: The Unraveling Chronicle — Worn Thread
acts.desc: Euryclea's quarters, Ithaca. A section of the funeral shroud Penelope wove and unpicked for three years — the most-rewoven section, worn by the nightly undoing. Euryclea cut it before Penelope burned the rest. History DC 11: understand why the worn thread is the evidence of the patience, not its failure.
acts.passText: You understand before she explains. She folds the cloth carefully.
acts.failText: You carry the cloth without grasping the distinction. Euryclea adds a note in her own hand.

acts.title: The Unraveling Chronicle — Technical Witness
acts.desc: Ithaca harbor road. A mainland weaver wants to provide a technical attestation that would classify the cloth as common linen rather than evidence — stripping its archival context. Insight DC 12: understand why her technical attestation is the wrong frame for the right observation.
acts.passText: You decline and explain. She is skeptical but lets you pass.
acts.failText: You accept. Her note is accurate and misses the point. You carry both.

acts.title: The Unraveling Chronicle — Historian's Collection
acts.desc: Corinthian road junction. A Lacedaemonian historian has a permission letter and wants the cloth for his private collection on Spartan women's textile practices. Penelope was an Ithacan queen, not a Spartan subject; the cloth belongs in the archive as evidence of a siege strategy, not a technical collection. Persuasion DC 13.
acts.passText: He accepts the distinction on the first exchange.
acts.failText: He follows for half a day before accepting. He notes your destination and says he will write to Weimar.

acts.title: The Unraveling Chronicle — Customs Inspection
acts.desc: Corinthian port customs dock. The inspector wants to assess duty on the cloth based on fiber quality. The cloth is a cultural record in archival transit, not commercial textile. Persuasion DC 11.
acts.passText: He accepts fine-woven. The cloth travels correctly stamped.
acts.failText: He stamps it second-grade. You pay the lesser duty. The cloth travels on with a misidentifying customs mark.

acts.title: The Unraveling Chronicle — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive intake. File Penelope's worn shroud fragment — three years of patience held in the thread-wear. The cloth is the evidence of a siege strategy that held a household for three years without weapons.
acts.passText: Sweelinck examines the wear in the thread. 'Three years of unwinding,' he says. 'The physical evidence of patience is usually consumed in the act of patience. This survived because the ruse was completed.' He files it under Defensive Strategies — Textile, First Entry.
acts.failText: Filed under Penelope's household materials. The cloth is in the archive.

acts.title: Eumaeus's Twenty Years — Faithful Count
acts.desc: Eumaeus's swineherd enclosure, Ithaca. The leather bag assembled for transit — worn clay tablets and scratched wooden tally sticks recording twenty years of livestock: stock counts, consumption records, the suitors' take per season. Kept without commission or legal authority. Insight DC 11: understand why informal tallies kept without expectation of use are more significant than a commissioned account would be.
acts.passText: You understand. Eumaeus nods once.
acts.failText: You take the bag without grasping the distinction. Philoetius adds a note about the ledger's informal status.

acts.title: Eumaeus's Twenty Years — Reparations Clerk
acts.desc: Ithaca estate registry annex. The reparations clerk wants to review the tallies before they leave — the reparations proceeding has not formally opened yet, but he is preemptively asserting a claim. Documents can be filed at the archive before a proceeding opens; once filed, certified copies can be returned. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: He accepts the distinction. The bag travels clean.
acts.failText: He notes the bag in his registry and gives you a transit document marking it 'evidence under review.' The archive receives it with the notation.

acts.title: Eumaeus's Twenty Years — Suitors' Factor
acts.desc: Adriatic ship. The representative of three suitors' families is on the same vessel. The tallies, if authenticated, are the only primary-source account of twenty years of consumption compiled without a legal motive — the hardest to challenge. He offers to buy the bag. The ledger is not for sale. Persuasion DC 11.
acts.passText: He accepts your first refusal. He says he will write to Weimar directly.
acts.failText: He increases the offer and shifts argument: he will commission a proper accounting that supersedes the informal tallies. You name the archive's primacy rule for first-filed primary documents. He withdraws.

acts.title: Eumaeus's Twenty Years — Ragusa Harbor
acts.desc: Ragusa harbor customs warehouse. The customs inspector wants the leather bag's contents individually inventoried. The tally sticks are unremarkable; the clay tablets can crack under standard cargo inspection procedures. The bag is an archival document in transit, not commercial cargo. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: He accepts the catalog approach and stamps the bag without opening it.
acts.failText: He handles three tablets before accepting the archival framing. None crack. The bag is sealed and stamped.

acts.title: Eumaeus's Twenty Years — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive intake. File Eumaeus's twenty-year livestock ledger — twenty years of informal accounts kept without commission or legal authority, because not keeping them seemed wrong.
acts.passText: Sweelinck opens the bag. He reads two tablets. 'Twenty years. Informal tallies. No commission, no legal authority, no expectation of use. He kept them because not keeping them seemed wrong.' He pauses. 'That is the entire reason. That is why this is in the archive.'
acts.failText: Filed under Faithful Household Accounts, Ithaca. The ledger is in the archive.

acts.title: Nausicaa's Letter — Palace Archivist
acts.desc: Phaeacia — Alcinous's palace archive room. The archivist Phaidon has held Nausicaa's sealed letter for three years — found in her private rooms after she married and moved away. A letter that was never sent: is it still a communication, or only a record of the moment of understanding it expressed? Insight DC 11.
acts.passText: You understand the distinction. He exhales. He does not add a note.
acts.failText: You take the tablet. The archivist adds a note about the discovery circumstances.

acts.title: Nausicaa's Letter — Alcinous's Steward
acts.desc: Scheria harbor. The palace steward intercepts you: a document bearing the royal seal — Alcinous's seal in miniature — is royal property. The letter was found in Nausicaa's private rooms, not the palace archives; it was written by a private person; the seal confirms origin, not ownership. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: He accepts the origin/ownership distinction. He notes in the harbor log: 'private document, archive transit.'
acts.failText: He holds the tablet forty-eight hours and consults a legal advisor. The advisor reaches the same conclusion. The tablet is released with a notation about the review.

acts.title: Nausicaa's Letter — Scholar at Rome
acts.desc: Rome. A Latin scholar with Greek philosophical training wants to read the unsent letter — carefully, not keep it. But the tablet is sealed. Opening it for scholarly consultation breaks the seal that is the document's authentication. He should write to the archive after filing. Insight DC 12.
acts.passText: You explain the archive procedure. He accepts and offers hospitality for the night.
acts.failText: He argues that the seal is already functionally opened because the archivist read the outer markings. You explain the difference between identification and opening. The seal is intact.

acts.title: Nausicaa's Letter — River Crossing
acts.desc: Flash flood on the river road north of Rome. The tablet is clay sealed in wax — sustained immersion in fast-moving water will lose the seal's impression, compromising authentication. Athletics DC 13 to carry it above water.
acts.passText: The tablet crosses dry. The seal is perfect.
acts.failText: One hand drops for a moment in the current. The wax takes water contact but the impression holds — barely. At the archive, Sweelinck notes the water mark but confirms the impression is still legible.

acts.title: Nausicaa's Letter — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck holds the sealed tablet — Nausicaa's letter, still sealed. He will not break it. The archive holds unsent letters as records of moments of understanding that required writing to become themselves.
acts.passText: He sets it carefully in the vault. He writes: 'Unsent Letters — Records Written for the Writer Rather Than the Reader, First Entry. Nausicaa's Letter: sealed; the archive will not open it; the seal is the document's authentication and its condition.' He closes the register.
acts.failText: Filed under Nausicaa, Phaeacian court documents. The letter is in the archive, sealed.

acts.title: Anticlea's Message — Second Scribe
acts.desc: Scribe's port storage. The second night's tablets — the underworld passage, Anticlea's account of Ithaca, the three attempts at embrace, the dispersion like a dream. The scribe held this chest separately. Insight DC 12: understand why testimony delivered by the dead has archival weight independent of its confirmability.
acts.passText: You understand. He nods. He closes the chest.
acts.failText: You carry the tablets without grasping the distinction. The scribe just watches you depart.

acts.title: Anticlea's Message — Philosopher's Challenge
acts.desc: Port harbor road. A sophist argues that testimony from the underworld is epistemologically inadmissible — the dead cannot be cross-examined; the account is unfalsifiable; the archive should not hold unfalsifiable documents as primary records. The tablets record what Odysseus reports; the archive notes the provenance. Persuasion DC 13.
acts.passText: He accepts the first framing. 'So the archive notes the problem.' You say: the archive notes the problem.
acts.failText: He follows for an hour before accepting the argument. He writes his objection in a note and asks you to carry it alongside the tablets. You do.

acts.title: Anticlea's Message — Telemachus's Request
acts.desc: Corinthian road. A courier from Telemachus arrives with a request to review the tablets before they are filed — he wants to know what Anticlea said about him. The tablets are not a family record; they are a public archival document; the archive's review process applies. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: The courier accepts the pre-filing review distinction. He makes a note and departs.
acts.failText: The courier sends a message to Telemachus. You continue without handing over the tablets. Two days later a second courier arrives saying Telemachus withdraws his request but asks you to note his concern in the delivery record. You do.

acts.title: Anticlea's Message — What She Said
acts.desc: Waystation south of Weimar. An old woman who lost her son to the sea asks what Anticlea said about Penelope — she wants to know if a dead mother's account of a wife's faithfulness is worth believing. Insight DC 11: understand what she actually needs from the conversation.
acts.passText: You tell her what you know. She asks: could Anticlea hold him. You say: he tried three times. No. She folds her hands again. She does not stop you.
acts.failText: You sit with her without opening the tablets. You tell her what you know of the passage from hearing it told. She thanks you.

acts.title: Anticlea's Message — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive intake. File Anticlea's testimony — complete, true, and received; the message delivered by the dead that cannot be confirmed because the sender is unavailable.
acts.passText: Sweelinck files the tablets. He writes: 'Testimony Delivered by the Dead — Unconfirmable Accounts, First Entry. Anticlea's Message: complete and internally consistent; the weight of being correctly told something by someone who cannot testify back is itself a category; the archive notes it.' He closes the ledger.
acts.failText: Filed under Odyssean Narration, underworld passage. The testimony is in the archive.

acts.title: The Cattle Account — Deduction Record
acts.desc: Scribe's port. The single cedar tablet from the Alcinous narration — the passage where Odysseus, having said he was asleep, attempts to reconstruct what was said before the cattle slaughter. The scribe noted at the top: 'He was not present. This is deduction, not witness.' History DC 11: understand why a sole survivor's reconstruction of the decision that made him the sole survivor is archivable.
acts.passText: You grasp the argument without the note. The scribe says: 'He had to try to understand it.' You nod.
acts.failText: You carry the tablet. The scribe adds a brief note: 'the sole survivor's reconstruction.'

acts.title: The Cattle Account — Families Who Were There
acts.desc: SIT harbor. Two relatives of sailors who died want to know what the tablet says — whether their kinsmen led the decision or were coerced. The reconstruction is Odysseus's deduction from aftermath evidence, not eyewitness testimony. Telling them the content before the archive contextualizes it gives them an unverified claim. Insight DC 12.
acts.passText: You explain the reconstruction's status — one man's deduction from aftermath evidence. They need to know what the archive's record will say, and the archive's record will say that clearly. They let you pass.
acts.failText: You explain you cannot share the content before filing. One of them reaches for the tablet. A struggle. The tablet is intact; you depart the harbor faster than planned.

acts.title: The Cattle Account — The Theologian
acts.desc: Rome. A Roman scholar argues the cattle of Hyperion are mythological vessels, not historical livestock; the slaughter is a religious event not subject to historical documentation. The tablet documents the hunger and reasoning of twelve men — not the theological dimension. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: He accepts the categorical distinction. He says he will write to Weimar.
acts.failText: He concedes the human dimension but adds to his register that the tablet should be cross-referenced with classical theological accounts. He lets you pass.

acts.title: The Cattle Account — Alps Crossing
acts.desc: Alpine pass. A mountain guide offers to carry the pack across the steepest section. Handing over the pack means the tablet is temporarily in someone else's custody. The custody hand-off is necessary but the chain should be unbroken in the archive account. Perception DC 11.
acts.passText: You watch each rest point. The pack stays sealed. The custody is clean.
acts.failText: At one rest point the guide opens the pack to redistribute weight. He cannot read Greek but the pack was opened. You note this.

acts.title: The Cattle Account — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive intake. File the Cattle Decision Reconstruction alongside Hyperion's divine complaint — the human-side record and the divine record of the same event. Together they are the most complete account available.
acts.passText: Sweelinck reads the scribe's note: 'He was not present. This is deduction, not witness.' He says: 'He was asleep. He woke to the smell of it. The archive files reconstructions separately from witnessed accounts. This one goes in the same vault as Hyperion's divine complaint.' He files. He writes: questComplete.
acts.failText: Filed under the Cattle Slaughter, Thrinacian voyage. The reconstruction is in the archive.

acts.title: The Captivity Record — Parcel from Phaeacia
acts.desc: Phaeacian harbor treasury. Unclaimed items from Odysseus's departure. At the back of a shelf: a parcel wrapped in oiled cloth, labeled in Hermes's hand — 'miscellaneous belongings, to follow.' Inside: the tally board, flat slab of driftwood, seven years of days scored in groups of ten. History DC 12: recognize the significance of a captive's private tally.
acts.passText: You understand immediately: this is Odysseus's account of his own captivity, kept for himself because there was no one else to keep it for. It is the only record that cannot be disputed by a god, because no god made it. You receive the Ogygia Tally Board.
acts.failText: You hold it a moment and set it down. The clerk wraps it back up. It will be noted in the departure inventory as 'one carved wooden board, origin unknown.' You take it anyway on the strength of a hunch, signing for it yourself.

acts.title: The Captivity Record — Goddess's Complaint
acts.desc: Phaeacian court archive. A certified copy of Calypso's divine grievance is here — the formal complaint she lodged with Zeus after Hermes came to her. Seven years, immortality offered and refused, release under compulsion. It describes the same seven years as the tally board from the opposite direction. Insight DC 12: both records must travel together.
acts.passText: You make the case that a captivity record consisting only of the captor's version is not a captivity record — it is a self-justification. The scribe releases a certified copy of Calypso's complaint to accompany the tally board north. You receive the Certified Copy of Calypso's Complaint.
acts.failText: The scribe decides to keep the divine complaint in the Phaeacian archive, where it belongs by provenance. You leave with the tally board only. The scribe makes a note: 'human record forwarded without divine counterpart; archivist discretion advised.'

acts.title: The Captivity Record — Nausicaa's Testimony
acts.desc: The palace garden at dusk. Nausicaa is sitting alone. She asks only one question: does the archive's record include any account of who found him on the beach. Only she holds the moment of re-entry into the human world. Persuasion DC 13.
acts.passText: She speaks for perhaps ten minutes. She describes the beach precisely — the olive tree, the salt on him, the way she kept her distance and called out as though to a man, not a wretch. She dictates a single paragraph for the archive. She does not ask for a copy. You receive Nausicaa's Beach Testimony.
acts.failText: She shakes her head gently. 'Let him tell it.' You move on. The record will be incomplete on that point. You note the gap.

acts.title: The Captivity Record — Ferryman's Question
acts.desc: River crossing south of Sithonia. A broad retired Phaeacian sailor at the ferry believes the tally board is a forgery — Odysseus was never a tally keeper, he says. He will not let you cross until you prove the board is genuine. Athletics DC 14: force the crossing.
acts.passText: You take the pole from him and hold the raft steady until he steps back. He looks at you for a long moment. 'All right,' he says. 'But if it's false, the gods know.' You cross. You receive the Ferryman's Crossing Token.
acts.failText: You go around. Two days lost, provisions short. The board travels in a damp pack and two of the score marks blur. You note the damage at the archive intake.

acts.title: The Captivity Record — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar. Sweelinck reads the tally board, the complaint copy, Nausicaa's paragraph. History DC 12: provide a complete provenance account — the damage, the gap in the arrival record, the circumstances of Calypso's complaint copy — so the intake record is accurate about what is known and what is inferred.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Ogygia Captivity Record: private tally board, seven years of days kept by the captive without witness; divine complaint filed against compelled release; arrival testimony from the woman who found him; gaps noted and preserved. The archive holds both sides of a captivity that no official document authorized and no god has since acknowledged.'
acts.failText: Sweelinck writes what you can give him. The gaps are noted as gaps. He files the board under 'Captivity Documents, Self-Reported, Unwitnessed.' He thanks you for what you brought.

acts.title: The Mast Agreement — Eurylochus's Widow
acts.desc: A farmhouse on the eastern slope of Ithaca. Eurylochus's widow has kept the Mast Binding Articles for twenty years — the tablets recording Odysseus's pre-Siren instructions: bind him, stop the crew's ears, ignore all release orders. Insight DC 12: understand what she needs before she will release the tablets — acknowledgment that the record is evidence of a wrong.
acts.passText: You sit down across from her and say: your husband was bound by an order he did not give, for a reason he had no part in, and died for following it. The archive needs the record of that. She is still for a long moment. Then she hands you the tablets without wrapping them. You receive the Mast Binding Articles.
acts.failText: You offer her compensation from the archive. She shakes her head. She covers the tablets again. 'He is dead. The tablets stay here.' You leave without them and must return via a different approach — she sends word a week later that she has thought it over and will give you a copy, not the original.

acts.title: The Mast Agreement — Surviving Sailor
acts.desc: Ithaca harbor. An old man mending nets — the only other survivor of the Thrinacian voyage. He jumped ship before the slaughter; no one knows who he is. He watched the Siren passage: Odysseus straining at the mast, the crew rowing faster when his brows signaled release. The corroborating witness. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: He speaks in a low voice for several minutes. He describes Odysseus's face at the mast precisely: calm until the song started, then something that needed a physical anchor to exist in at all. He dictates a statement. You receive the Survivor's Corroboration.
acts.failText: He says nothing happened that he wants to talk about. He goes on mending nets. You leave a wax tablet with a brief note and your name, in case he changes his mind. He does not, but you note his existence in the intake report.

acts.title: The Mast Agreement — Philosopher's Objection
acts.desc: Constantinople. A Byzantine logician argues: a man cannot bind himself to an agreement that overrides his own subsequent commands; authority cannot be delegated against itself. He holds the tablets as he speaks. Persuasion DC 13: the agreement is archivable precisely because of its paradox — the pre-authorization makes it a contract.
acts.passText: He thinks for a long time. 'The pre-authorization makes it a contract,' he says slowly. 'The captain made himself an object governed by an agreement he authored. The document is the agreement, not the action.' He stamps a provenance certificate. You receive the Provenance Certificate.
acts.failText: He sets the tablets down. 'I will note my reservation.' He writes a letter of objection to accompany the tablets, which you accept. The archive will hold both.

acts.title: The Mast Agreement — River at Night
acts.desc: A river crossing north of Constantinople, deep in the night watch. Three grieving relatives of Thrinacian sailors wait at the bridge — they want to know if the tablets name who ate first, who argued hardest. Athletics DC 14: hold the bridge; it is narrow and the ground is yours.
acts.passText: You hold the bridge until they back away from the dark and the water rushing below. No one speaks. They leave. You cross. The tablets are intact. You receive the Night Bridge Crossing Mark.
acts.failText: They get the tablets for one hour before you recover them. They read what they were looking for — Eurylochus's name is in the agreement. They put the tablets back. You continue. The tablets have been read by unauthorized parties; you note it.

acts.title: The Mast Agreement — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar. Sweelinck reads the tablets. History DC 12: give a complete intake account — widow, harbor, Constantinople, bridge — so the archive holds the human record of an agreement that governed a god-level event.
acts.passText: You lay out every element in sequence: widow, harbor, Constantinople, bridge. Sweelinck writes it all down. He says: 'The Sirens' island is the poem's black box. We have the agreement that made the hearing possible, and a sole survivor who has not said what the song contained. The archive notes this silence as data.' He files. You receive the Archive Receipt.
acts.failText: Sweelinck files the tablets with a note of partial provenance. The survivor's corroboration is filed separately as an unverified witness account. The record is functional but incomplete.

acts.title: The Beggar's Passport — Eumaeus's Hut
acts.desc: Eumaeus's upland station, Ithaca. The beggar's wallet on a post by the door — battered leather, two pieces of bread, a flask of oil, a small knife, and a folded insert with written false identities. Found on the dung heap after the slaughter. He kept the cover story intact for twenty hours; without that custody the disguise fails and the suitors survive. Insight DC 12.
acts.passText: You tell him: he was the first archive this object had. He kept the cover story intact for twenty hours. Without that custody the disguise fails and the suitors survive. He looks at you for a long moment. Then he takes the wallet off the post and holds it out. You receive the Beggar's Wallet.
acts.failText: He hands it over without ceremony. 'Take it. It was never mine.' He goes back to his leather. You have the wallet but the intake notes will reflect that the chain of custody explanation was not completed.

acts.title: The Beggar's Passport — Nurse's Account
acts.desc: Palace women's quarters. Euryclea recognized him in the dark — the lamp angle, the thigh, the scar she remembered from when he was eight years old. She knew for twelve hours and told no one. Her recognition account is the only record of those twelve hours. Persuasion DC 12.
acts.passText: She talks for half an hour. She describes the lamp, the angle of his thigh, the specific shape of the scar. She says: 'I had him. Then I had him again. Twenty years apart, the same.' She dictates a clean account for the archive. You receive Euryclea's Recognition Statement.
acts.failText: She says nothing about the twelve hours. She gives you a dry recitation of the footwashing, the scar, the grip. 'He said nothing. I said nothing.' The record is factually accurate and misses the weight entirely.

acts.title: The Beggar's Passport — Cover Story's Contradictions
acts.desc: Palace steward's room. Odysseus told three different versions of his cover story to three different listeners — Eumaeus, Telemachus, Penelope. The steward Medon has noted the contradictions and is deciding whether they invalidate the record. History DC 13: the variations are evidence of adaptation to audience, not inconsistency.
acts.passText: Medon pauses, then begins to write very carefully. 'He told Eumaeus one thing, Telemachus a second, Penelope a third — and in each case the thing he told them was what that person most needed to believe was possible.' He files all three versions with annotations. You receive the Three-Version Cover Record.
acts.failText: Medon files the most internally consistent version and notes the discrepancies as copying errors. The record is tidy and wrong.

acts.title: The Beggar's Passport — Antinous's Household
acts.desc: Eupeithes's house. Two men are trying to seize the beggar's wallet — they want the folded oiled-leather insert with the written false identities. If they get the insert, the written element of the cover story is lost. Athletics DC 14: keep the wallet sealed.
acts.passText: You take the blow and keep moving — out through the courtyard gate before they can organize a second approach. The wallet stays sealed. The insert is intact. You receive the Intact Wallet Seal.
acts.failText: They get the wallet long enough to remove the folded oiled-leather insert with the written false identities. When you recover it, the insert is gone. The wallet is intact. The written element of the cover story is lost. You note the loss.

acts.title: The Beggar's Passport — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive — provenance account of the disguise's primary object. The beggar's wallet that may be the most precisely accurate representation of its owner in the entire collection. History DC 12.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Twenty years of real wandering made the prop indistinguishable from the man. The archive holds a beggar's wallet that may be the most precisely accurate representation of its owner in the entire collection.' He files. You receive the Archive Receipt.
acts.failText: Sweelinck files what he has. The gaps are noted. The wallet is catalogued under 'Disguise Artifacts, Self-Authored Identity, Ithaca.'

acts.title: The Bed That Could Not Be Moved — Palace Accounts
acts.desc: Palace accounts room, Ithaca. A water-damaged shelf, stacked warped tablets. Dolius's son is holding one very carefully — a tablet filed as 'bedroom allocation' by the scribe who witnessed the recognition. It contains: Penelope's instruction to move the bed, Odysseus's eruption of specific knowledge about the olive tree bedpost, Penelope's response. History DC 12: identify its significance.
acts.passText: You explain what the tablet contains to Dolius's son in two sentences. He hands it to you immediately, carefully, with both hands. 'I thought something had happened,' he says. 'I didn't know what.' You receive the Penelope Test Tablet.
acts.failText: You recognize the exchange but cannot immediately place it in context. Dolius's son keeps the tablet for now, pending your return. You come back the following day with enough knowledge to name it correctly.

acts.title: The Bed That Could Not Be Moved — Penelope's Version
acts.desc: The queen's upper room, late afternoon. Penelope is at her loom, shuttle in hand. The tablet records the proof. It does not record the inside of the test: why the bed specifically; what she was listening for in his voice before the content; the twenty years of evidence that made this test definitive. Persuasion DC 13.
acts.passText: She sets the shuttle down. She speaks quietly and at length. She describes what the bed means: made by his own hands, the foundation of the house, rooted in the earth of the courtyard. No impersonator could know it. 'He didn't argue,' she says. 'He stated.' She dictates a paragraph. You receive Penelope's Interior Account.
acts.failText: She looks at you for a long time. 'The tablet is enough,' she says. She goes back to her loom. You leave with the tablet and a gap in the record. The archive will note it.

acts.title: The Bed That Could Not Be Moved — Laertes in the Vineyard
acts.desc: The farm outside Ithaca, midday. Laertes in the vineyard, staking a vine. He will talk about the trees. He is not sure he will talk about the test — before the recognition, Odysseus gave him a false identity and watched him weep for his own son. Insight DC 12: acknowledge this before asking him to narrate it.
acts.passText: You acknowledge, before asking anything, that being tested by your own child is a thing the archive cannot judge and does not need to frame. He is still a moment. Then he talks about the full hour. He says: 'I knew it was him when he started lying that well.' He dictates. You receive Laertes' Recognition Account.
acts.failText: You ask about the trees. He names all thirteen pear trees, the ten apple trees, the forty fig trees, the fifty rows of vines, in order, from memory. He gives you a clean account of the recognition. He does not mention the false identity or the hour he wept before Odysseus told the truth.

acts.title: The Bed That Could Not Be Moved — Bow as Instrument
acts.desc: Palace armory. The bow-maker's son — claiming the bow as an inherited piece since Iphitus was murdered — is attempting to remove it with two men. The tablet confirming Odysseus's identity also confirms his claim to every object in the palace. Athletics DC 14: prevent the removal of the bow.
acts.passText: You put yourself between the men and the bow rack and stay there until they consult with their legal advisor and find their case is weaker than they thought. They leave. The bow stays. You receive the Bow Remains in Place Certificate.
acts.failText: They take the bow. It will be subject to legal proceedings. The archive notes the connection between the tablet and the bow's contested provenance, and files accordingly. The recognition record is intact; the physical instrument of proof is disputed.

acts.title: The Bed That Could Not Be Moved — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar. Sweelinck reads the tablet in full, Penelope's interior account, Laertes' full hour. History DC 13: assemble the complete provenance — tablet provenance, Penelope's design of the test, Laertes' full version including the false-identity hour, the bow's contested status.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes for a long time. He says finally: 'The bed cannot be moved. The archive cannot hold the bed. What the archive holds is the record of a man who knew a thing about a bed that no one else could know, and said it without thinking, and was recognized by that saying. The document is the speaking. We file it as such.' He files. He writes: questComplete.
acts.failText: Sweelinck files what you have with noted gaps. The record is significant but partial. He thanks you for what you brought.
